content: Fibroadenoma of the breast is a benign tumor that arises due to the proliferation of both glandular and stromal elements. Fibroadenomas can be classified into four subtypes based on microscopic histopathological analysis: juvenile fibroadenoma, complex fibroadenoma, myxoid fibroadenoma, and cellular fibroadenoma. Fibroadenoma is a common benign breast tumor that originates from connective tissue cells. These cells typically provide functional and mechanical support to the surrounding tissues. Fibroadenomas are sensitive to estrogen and progesterone, and they may grow during pregnancy. The MED12 gene is the most frequently implicated gene in the pathogenesis of fibroadenoma. Gross pathological examination of fibroadenomas reveals a rubbery, tan-colored, and lobulated mass. Microscopically, fibroadenomas exhibit a biphasic proliferation of stromal and epithelial components, which can be arranged in two distinct growth patterns: pericanalicular and intracanalicular. The exact cause of fibroadenoma is unknown. However, it is important to differentiate fibroadenomas from other conditions with similar clinical presentations, such as phyllodes tumors, hamartomas, and adenomyoepitheliomas. Fibroadenoma is the most common breast mass in adolescent women in the United States. While there is no definitive data on its exact incidence in the general U.S. population, it predominantly affects individuals under 30 years of age. Females are more commonly affected than males, and fibroadenomas are more frequently observed in individuals of African American descent compared to Caucasians. Risk factors for developing fibroadenomas include obesity, estrogen replacement therapy, and nulliparity. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) states that there is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening for fibroadenomas. Most patients with fibroadenomas are asymptomatic. If untreated, fibroadenomas may develop into painless, mobile, and well-circumscribed breast lumps. These tumors are benign and rarely lead to complications. They often enlarge during pregnancy and regress after menopause. The prognosis for fibroadenomas is excellent, with a five-year survival rate nearly equivalent to that of the general population. The hallmark clinical feature of fibroadenoma is a painless, firm, solitary, mobile, and slow-growing lump in the breast. Physical examination typically reveals a well-circumscribed, firm, and mobile breast mass. Imaging studies can aid in the diagnosis of fibroadenomas. On CT scans, fibroadenomas appear as oval masses with well-defined borders, a lobulated appearance, and localized calcifications. MRI findings on T1-weighted images show a well-defined, isointense mass, often located in the upper-outer quadrant of the breast. Ultrasound findings include a well-circumscribed, round to ovoid, macrolobulated mass that is generally uniformly hypoechoic. Mammograms may reveal a well-circumscribed, discrete, oval mass that is isodense to breast glandular tissue, sometimes containing coarse popcorn calcifications. The definitive diagnosis of fibroadenoma is confirmed through an ultrasound-guided biopsy. Microscopic histopathological analysis reveals characteristic findings that confirm the diagnosis. Most cases of fibroadenoma are self-limiting and require only close follow-up. Surgical intervention is typically reserved for patients older than 35 years of age or in cases where the fibroadenoma exhibits atypical features.
